Assessing monthly annual consumption in Tampa, FL, it was found that heating-mode savings are limited to December, January, and February (Figure 44). Given the hot, humid climate in Tampa, FL, greater energy savings are possible by using HP-TES in cooling mode only. Comparisons were also made to recharge energy consumption. Throughout the shoulder and winter seasons, the recharge energy required is lower than both the TES discharge and baseline energy due to moderate overnight temperatures, which reduce the temperature lift during the recharge cycle. However, higher summer nocturnal temperatures force the HP-TES cycle to recharge at higher temperature lifts, increasing recharge energy requirements and challenging total load-shifting. Given that NYC has cold winters, the standalone baseline system could not provide the nominal 14 kW of heating capacity, and backup heating (COP ≤ 1) is required. The simulated HP- TES can provide heating capacity of 15 – 17 kW during peak periods without the need for auxiliary heating, resulting in peak demand reductions of up to 50% during the coldest winter months (Figure 45). During the summer, demand reduction ranged from 10% to 25%, depending on outdoor temperature. The main challenge with summer operations in NYC is the high energy requirements for recharging, driven by high nocturnal temperatures. While this may not have a direct cost to an end-user (the off-peak rate is 10% of the on-peak rate [100]), this energy requirement may strain the grid during off- peak hours. Thus, recharge energy mitigation strategies are required [104].
